outline.description: Sets out the factual setting, who the players are, what AFL asked for, how OSC and the district court responded, and how the case arrived at the D.C. Circuit with Article III standing as the dispositive issue.
subtopics: AFL’s FOIA request to DOJ for emails related to judicial recusals; DOJ’s asserted practice of not searching employee emails without the employee’s consent; separate FOIA suit resulting in ongoing productions not at issue here
AFL’s complaint to the Office of Special Counsel (OSC) alleging an arbitrary FOIA withholding policy and invoking 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3)
OSC’s refusal to investigate based on FOIA § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) predicates not being met

District court’s ruling: § 1216 authority not limited by § 552(a)(4)(F)(i); OSC’s initial legal error; court nonetheless declined to compel investigation as discretionary under § 1216(c); remand to OSC; OSC again declined; final judgment entered
Appeal to the D.C. Circuit; standard of review de novo; court ordered supplemental briefing on Article III standing, which neither party initially addressed

outline.chapter_title: Statutory Framework: OSC, the CSRA, and FOIA’s Separate OSC Trigger
outline.description: Explains the legal architecture governing OSC’s authority and procedures, the relationship between CSRA provisions (§§ 1214–1216), and FOIA’s distinct OSC-triggering provision.
subtopics: OSC’s role under the Civil Service Reform Act: investigative/prosecutorial functions to promote a lawfully conducted civil service (Frazier v. MSPB); enforcement before the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB)
Section 1214 (corrective action for prohibited personnel practices) and § 1215 (disciplinary action): available remedies and § 1214’s complainant notification procedures

Section 1216(a)(3): OSC shall investigate allegations of arbitrary/capricious FOIA withholdings; § 1216(c) allows OSC to seek corrective/disciplinary action ‘in the same way as if’ a prohibited personnel practice were involved
FOIA § 552(a)(4)(F)(i): separate mandatory OSC proceeding triggered only after a court orders production, awards fees, and questions arbitrary/capricious withholding
Whether § 1214 procedures apply to § 1216 investigations: recognized as discretionary, not mandatory (e.g., Carson v. OSC)

outline.description: Lays out the constitutional standing requirements, the special posture of procedural and informational injuries, and the plaintiff’s burden at the pleading stage.
subtopics: Article III case-or-controversy: injury in fact (concrete, particularized, actual or imminent), causation, and redressability (Lujan)

Procedural injury framework: relaxed imminence and redressability only if tied to a threatened concrete interest; injury in fact and causation remain required (Center for Law & Education; Florida Audubon)
No standing for a procedural right in vacuo (Summers; Citizens for Constitutional Integrity)
Informational standing: plaintiff must be denied information a statute entitles them to receive (Akins; Public Citizen; ASPCA; Zivotofsky)
Pleading-stage burden: plausible factual allegations for each element (Food & Water Watch); appellate court’s obligation to ensure jurisdiction (Steel Co.)

outline.chapter_title: Applying Standing to AFL’s FOIA-Records Theory
outline.description: Analyzes AFL’s contention that OSC’s refusal to investigate caused AFL not to receive DOJ records, focusing on traceability and redressability defects.
subtopics: AFL’s theory: OSC’s failure to investigate under § 1216 prevented DOJ from producing records requested under FOIA
Traceability: any informational injury from non-disclosure is attributable to DOJ, not OSC

Speculative causal chain: OSC might investigate; might pursue § 1214/§ 1215 action; MSPB might sanction; DOJ might then produce records—reliance on independent third-party decisions (FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine)
Limits on compelling agency enforcement discretion (Heckler v. Chaney)

Redressability must turn on relief binding the parties, not the potential persuasive effect on nonparties (Haaland v. Brackeen); need for a ‘very likely’ link to spur next steps (Hecate Energy v. FERC)
Result: no standing under the first theory due to failures of causation and redressability

outline.chapter_title: Applying Standing to AFL’s OSC-Information Theory; Disposition and Significance
outline.description: Evaluates AFL’s separate informational-injury claim premised on receiving investigation notices/updates, explains why it fails, and sets out the court’s disposition and lessons.
subtopics: AFL’s claim to investigation-related information: argues an interest in notices and updates akin to § 1214 if OSC investigates under § 1216
No statutory entitlement: § 1216(a)(3) may require investigating but does not entitle complainants to receive information; informational standing fails without such entitlement
Discretionary application of § 1214 procedures in § 1216 investigations (Carson): absence of mandatory notice obligations defeats a concrete informational injury
Redressability: even ordering a § 1216 investigation would not likely yield § 1214-type notices, given OSC’s discretion
Disposition: AFL lacks Article III standing; the D.C. Circuit vacates the district court’s judgment and remands with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction

Significance: underscores barriers to using another agency’s enforcement process to remedy a third party’s FOIA denial; procedural/informational standing requires a clear statutory entitlement and relief that binds the defendant; courts avoid speculative chains involving independent actors
